We are getting this numbers from profiles. So this is only analyzing goroutines that actually needed expansion (any goroutine that was lower than starting stack size won't show in the profile), so yeah this is only mean of goroutines exceeeding current mean.

Ok, so that makes me think that your goroutine stack size distribution is bimodal. It looks like the average size here is below 4KB (because that's the size the runtime chose for a starting stack), but for the goroutines whose stack exceeds 4KB, they are quite a bit larger.

> For now, we have a per-service knob that overwrites those values and have been rolling overrides to either 16kb or 32kb for the top services. Those changes worked as expected, we see dramatic CPU drop and corresponding stack memory increase - in our case it’s usually <200mb of memory and it’s acceptable for those services as their heap sizes are much larger.

Does the 200MB space increase include the space for the small stacks getting larger, or does it just count the space from the big stacks getting larger?
How large is the total heap?

Possibly one way to go here is to increase the starting stack size to, say, the 75th percentile of existing stack sizes, or even the 90th percentile, if the total size for all stacks would remain under, say, 1% of the total heap size. By bounding to the total heap size we ensure that the extra stack space we waste is not significant overall in the application.

And we could always use more optimization of the stack copying itself. I don't think anyone has looked at it in quite a while.

One idea on the top of my head was... We already track GC cpu time and Scavenger cpu time... Could we do something similar for stack growth? Like if current cpu time is <1% do nothing, but if it is >1% instead of using mean use p75... If it is not enough do p90 and so on. That way we are only impacting applications that see a lot of stack growth (I know we put limitation to things like the scavenger, but not sure how much effort is to do this).

It might be just easier to do a simple higher percentile though.

On Thursday in #57175, one of the Uber folks said for their data:

> The problem with the global average seems to be primarily long-dormant goroutines skewing the average.

Based on that, I have a local change that attempts to change the average stack size calculation to ignore goroutines that have been inactive for ~one GC cycle. 

That seems to reduce CPU usage in a synthetic benchmark with many small inactive goroutines with other goroutines that grow the stack. 

I need to do a little bit more sanity checking, but I will probably send a CL for discussion (maybe either later tonight or maybe tomorrow). 

It’s very much exploratory and intended to help move the conversation forward. 

Maybe another solution is better, or maybe something like that makes sense in addition to some other change, like looking at percentiles.

@randall77 yeah bimodal makes sense.

After your message (sorry, we should have given those details from the start), I looked at the "service 1" that you quoted. Randomly samping a single instance I see 3678 goroutines.

There are:
-  480 `google.golang.org/grpc/internal/grpcsync.(*CallbackSerializer)` with tiny stack
- - I don't grok grpc enough yet to know what this is, but it seems relatively silly - most of these goroutines are alive since the start of the service
- around 440 of our internal kafka publisher library that seems to spin up 10 worker goroutines per destination topic (new discovery right now). The stack is very shallow there.
- 702 goroutines in `internal/poll.runtime_pollWait` 
- 216 goroutines in `base/chrono/periodic.(*defaultRunner).execAndWait` - basically a timer, I would expect to be various internal libraries "refreshing their caches."
- around 200 in `google.golang.org/grpc/internal/transport.*` with also fairly shallow stack
- 312 in `tchannel-go.(*Connection).writeFrames` - like above.

> Does the 200MB space increase include the space for the small stacks getting larger, or does it just count the space from the big stacks getting larger?
> How large is the total heap?

This would largely depend on the application - the one quoted above (with the biggest growth, where we override the dynamic growth with 32kb) had a memory limit of 48gb.
The 200MB was just a growth in stack size, that service happend to have around 7000-8000 goroutines per instance.

It seems both:
- only count active goroutines, or
- only count goroutines that died recently (to ignore the background ones, which really shouldn't be affecting the starting ones size?)

are likely to be a good heuristic.  

This also means explains why grafana/mimir#7131 worked well. We have a few entry points like the grpc one (a "worker" framework that spawns goroutines, a "safego" framework that wraps goroutines to recover panics (😞 )). If we added goroutine pools there, we could feasibly minimize the impact as well.

Isn't there a fundamental issue with picking a default stack size for all goroutines? I've wondered whether it would be advantageous/worthwhile to dynamically track the default stack size for each "go" statement.

Crude idea: statically allocate a uint64 to track the preferred intiial stack size for each `go` location. Each `g` should have a pointer to the dynamic initial stack size for it's launch location. The _first_ time a the GC runs for that `g` it merges the current stable size back into the initial stack size, perhaps similar to a load average (ratio of old value and new value). If many goroutines are launched it should coverge to something useful/fairly stable for that location. There are a lot of design choices here that could give better performance. PGO could also set the default stack size for each location (but this might end up being a smaller optimisation).

Some code designs can still result in multi-modal initial stack sizes for a given `go` location (eg, generic worker pools). Per-`go` statement tracking won't solve that, but it should give the code auther the option to change their design so stack sizes aren't multi-modal for a particular location if it matters to them.

>  I've wondered whether it would be advantageous/worthwhile to dynamically track the default stack size for each "go" statement.

Hi @mpx, FWIW, I think there was some discussion of that type of approach in #18138, including possibly tracking by goroutine start PC or multiple frames. I think there was also a draft CL.

See also [this comment](
https://github.com/golang/go/issues/18138#issuecomment-1804326857
) from that issue from Michael P. regarding gRPC, which includes:

> As far as I can tell [1], gRPC starts this per-request goroutine before determining which request it is handling. This means that no matter the amount of context the runtime uses prior to starting the goroutine, it won't be able to deterministically differentiate between the different types of requests.

That's not to say the approach is not possible or not worthwhile to consider. I mostly just wanted to point to some of the prior discussion.

In the end, it might make sense to make more than one improvement around this overall problem, which might better help handle a broader set of cases.

As a brief update, I also now have a local change that estimates a p75 stack size (based on Keith's comment [above](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/77893#issuecomment-3987174127)). 

I have a temporary `GODEBUG=gcstacksizemode=x` that picks between:
* the old behavior (`gcstacksizemode=0`), vs.
* excluding inactive goroutines and using the average of the remaining goroutines (`gcstacksizemode=1`, which is what I described on Monday [above](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/77893#issuecomment-3987363994)), vs.
* excluding inactive goroutines and using the p75 size of the remaining goroutines (`gcstacksizemode=2`)

Some synthetic benchmarks seem to respond positively.

I'll probably send it as 2 CLs to help with discussion of alternatives.

I did not yet do anything like checking if using the p75 stack size would result in an estimated stack usage of more than 1% of total heap (also Keith's comment [above](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/77893#issuecomment-3987174127)), but that seems feasible if it is desired.

Tangential - a new idea came up with "generational stack sizing". If we assume that anything older than X minutes is a background goroutine that already runs at the desired size, we could treat it as irrelevant and ignore it in the math. This would address the binomial nature of the workloads, but I don't know if this is easier to implement or even desirable.

Change https://go.dev/cl/758141 mentions this issue: `runtime: exclude inactive goroutines from starting stack size heuristic`

FWIW, I mailed two related CLs, with [CL 758141](https://go.dev/cl/758141) currently being the more interesting one.

In that CL, it adjusts the heuristic to attempt to exclude inactive goroutines when estimating what stack size a new goroutine might need. 

The theory is that a goroutine that has been dormant ~1-2 GC cycles is likely not as predictive of how a new goroutine will grow its stack size. ~~Also, dormant goroutines might have had their stacks shrunk across multiple GC cycles~~. (_edit_: sorry, the stack shrinking probably doesn't matter for this CL, though long dormant goroutines likely do tend to be small based on where they become dormant.)

My understanding of the data from Uber is that inactive goroutines might have been pulling down the stack size estimate, though I guess still TBD how much of a factor that was for Uber in practice.

The exact approach the CL takes for determining "recently active" is slightly nuanced, but probably not too hard to adjust that if needed.

Sample benchmark results show some improvement. See the [CL 758141](https://go.dev/cl/758141) commit message for a description of this benchmark with some brief commentary. (In short, this benchmark creates many large goroutines. In the old column, adding 1k small goroutines slows down the overall benchmark, but with the changes in my CL in the new column, the "many small goroutines" penalty seems to mostly go away for this benchmark at least.)

```
goos: linux
pkg: runtime
                         │    old-10s.out    │    new-cl-758141-10s.out │
                         │   sec/op          │   sec/op     vs base     │

Issue18138/all-large-4         327.5µ ± 2%     308.1µ ± 1%   -5.93% (p=0.000 n=20)
Issue18138/1k-small-4          352.9µ ± 1%     307.2µ ± 1%  -12.94% (p=0.000 n=20)
```

I also have two other candidate changes that I haven't mailed yet (including calculating p75/p90 sizes and a separate more aggressive change), but [CL 758141](https://go.dev/cl/758141) is the least complicated approach of those candidates. 

My sense from reading some of the history is that Keith likely would prefer a simpler approach if possible, so it could make sense to try testing that CL out to see how much it helps in practice (maybe in some staging area or similar?). Maybe that CL is enough, or maybe not (and if not, I can tidy up and sanity check the others a bit more and probably mail those too to help with the discussion).

Thanks @thepudds!

Quick update: I've tested this on 2 different services (infra services, not part of the analysis pasted above) in staging (has much lower traffic), and the results weren't positive. The `runtime.copystack` costs went up a bit, and I'm seeing small increase (<1%) on  `runtime.shrinkstack`. 

However, testing the [NumStreamWorkers](https://pkg.go.dev/google.golang.org/grpc#NumStreamWorkers) on one of the above service, resulted in ~100% elimination of `runtime.copystack` costs. 

I will be testing this patch on more services and will give you an update here soon.

Hi @geekswaroop, thanks for trying out [CL 758141](https://go.dev/cl/758141)!

If it's not too much hassle, I think it would probably be worthwhile to get at least some output from the new `GODEBUG=gcstacksizetrace=1` using that CL on one of those representative services (e.g., maybe something like `GODEBUG=gcstacksizetrace=1,gctrace=1` for something like 10-20 GC cycles using that CL).

That could give some data around whether or not there are many idle goroutines in that service, or maybe it could be a hint there is something wrong in the CL, or maybe it's just the CL is not a sufficient improvement to the heuristics, but the more detailed data output while using it would likely be interesting.

Separately, earlier today I mailed [CL 764220](https://go.dev/cl/764220) as a potential alternative. Right now, it defaults to tracking and calculating a p90, and uses the larger of the average or the p90 size. The synthetic benchmark again shows improvement, but the real question of course is whether it would help the real-world services at Uber based on their specific characteristics. That CL defaults to p90 to make it easier to test, but it also supports p75 if you do `GODEBUG=adaptivestackstart=2` (with the details in the commit message).

Right now, at least my intent would be to see if it moves the needle.  

If it ends up being appealing, we might also need to make it dynamically fall back to average and/or dynamically switch between something like p95 vs. p75 vs. average (e.g., Keith had suggested perhaps something like a 1% cap on estimated stack memory use prior to perhaps falling back to a more conservative heuristic). I think that would be a ~minor change, but probably worth seeing if it helps first.

It would probably be interesting to also see `GODEBUG=gcstacksizetrace=1` for that newer CL.

One other possible next step after this might be combining the earlier [CL 758141](https://go.dev/cl/758141) (paying attention to active vs. inactive goroutines) with the newer [CL 764220](https://go.dev/cl/764220) (p90/p75).  But probably worth seeing the next round of data first, I would guess.

> Hi @mpx, FWIW, I think there was some discussion of that type of approach in https://github.com/golang/go/issues/18138, including possibly tracking by goroutine start PC or multiple frames. I think there was also a draft CL.

Not sure if you are referring to my old experiment (https://github.com/golang/go/issues/18138#issuecomment-452958767, https://github.com/golang/go/issues/18138#issuecomment-901461900, [CL](https://go-review.googlesource.com/c/go/+/341990)) but if so I still think that (at least) per-starting-PC estimation would be useful especially in larger applications (e.g. where there are multiple main spawning points for goroutines).

One thing that I would definitely add to my old CL is considering not just the PC, but also the address of the function/method/closure passed to the `go` statement (to correctly handle the `workgroup.Go`/`errgroup.Go` pattern), falling back to PC-only on miss.

Few findings I think are useful for discussion:

1) Bimodal distribution is universal across our services
2) Most of these goroutines, once grown, stays grown
3) The patch can't help when the bimodal tail is small. 

I'd lean on implementing a combination of your patch, as it helps bimodal shaped workloads. Curious to hear your thoughts

An update on our progress, with the realization that:
- the GC frequency is so much higher than the goroutine life duration and
- the large number of background goroutines (thousands) with minimal stack

It seemed approaches targeted at measuring active goroutines, no matter the percentile, are bound to fail.

We're currently testing a basically one-liner patch 

```diff
---
 src/runtime/proc.go | 54 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++----------------
 1 file changed, 35 insertions(+), 19 deletions(-)

diff --git src/runtime/proc.go src/runtime/proc.go
index 005c875cbf..09cb577d34 100644
--- src/runtime/proc.go
+++ src/runtime/proc.go
@@ -5469,8 +5469,24 @@ func gfput(pp *p, gp *g) {
 
 	stksize := gp.stack.hi - gp.stack.lo
 
-	if stksize != uintptr(startingStackSize) {
-		// non-standard stack size - free it.
+	if stksize > 131072 {
 		stackfree(gp.stack)
 		gp.stack.lo = 0
 		gp.stack.hi = 0
@@ -5527,21 +5543,22 @@ retry:
 	if gp == nil {
 		return nil
 	}
-	if gp.stack.lo != 0 && gp.stack.hi-gp.stack.lo != uintptr(startingStackSize) {
-		// Deallocate old stack. We kept it in gfput because it was the
-		// right size when the goroutine was put on the free list, but
-		// the right size has changed since then.
-		systemstack(func() {
-			stackfree(gp.stack)
-			gp.stack.lo = 0
-			gp.stack.hi = 0
-			gp.stackguard0 = 0
-			if valgrindenabled {
-				valgrindDeregisterStack(gp.valgrindStackID)
-				gp.valgrindStackID = 0
-			}
-		})
-	}
```

The reasoning is:
- we want to bias towards "recently dead" goroutines as they are likely similar to the incoming one
- stack shrinking will "fix down" any oversizing
- we're not making a goroutine bomb situation worse:
  - the "peak" memory utilization shouldn't change 
  - [markrootGFreeStacks](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/d1d68c2dd09a74a233163448f6af5ac4f6a4c0fc/src/runtime/mgcmark.go#L359) should prevent any unbounded growth.

So far the results are promising, will report back in a week or two.
Change https://go.dev/cl/793780 mentions this issue: `runtime: cache grown goroutine stacks to reduce stack-growth cost`
Change https://go.dev/cl/793920 mentions this issue: `runtime: add stack size watermark for initial stack size heuristic`

Hi @geekswaroop and @rabbbit, I'll take a look at the CL you sent!

FWIW, I also mailed my "more aggressive" [CL 793920](https://go.dev/cl/793920) that I had mentioned a while back. (Or I guess maybe re-mailed, I see I actually had sent it back in May as one of my "scratch/test" CLs to run against the trybots).

This is more of a "belt and suspenders" solution, but it might be overkill, and we might only need just the belt or just the suspenders, or maybe a simpler solution. 

It does gather a decent amount of what I think are fairly useful stats, though, which is one reason I'm curious if it will be possible to try this out before too long, along with seeing whether it captures most of the possible benefit.

In this CL, it is getting a ~10x performance improvement in the synthetic benchmarks, vs. my two earlier alternative CLs were getting more like ~15%, and the logs with this CL show the initial stack size ends up tracking the needed stack size almost perfectly for the synthetic benchmarks.

On master, the stack sizing is sampling goroutine sizes during GC, which means it doesn't often see the peak goroutine size, and also can miss some short-lived goroutines.

In contrast, in [CL 793920](https://go.dev/cl/793920), it:
1. tracks the peak size explicitly via a stack size watermark (hopefully cheaply)
2. tracks when a goroutine was created (in terms of GC cycle)
3. records what was the peak size for new goroutines when they die (so records even for short-lived goroutines) and also during the scan (where "new" is currently defined as created within last 5 GC cycles, though that could be tweaked)

I think it'd likely be possible to simplify. Currently there are three new uint8 fields on the goroutine (snuck in via gaps in the alignment to avoid growing the `g`), but I think almost any subset of those three could be made useful, and I've tried for example not tracking age, or only tracking age but not the peak stack usage and just using the current allocated stack size at death (which can be smaller than the overall peak based on shrinking per GC, but the youngest goroutines have the least shrinking, so maybe that's OK).

Here is an example of the current stats. Here, you can see the scanned average is 2KiB (basically the behavior on master / Go 1.26), while the stack size watermark avg is 601KiB, and the stack size watermark percentiles tell the story of the peak stack size distribution for the measured new goroutines. The start of the line shows it using the p75 peak size value (2048KiB) for new goroutines (based on the GODEBUG setting used here):

```
stack sizing: @9.129s 2048K stack start size, 2K scanned avg for 1019 stacks, 601K watermark avg for 1425 stacks
 (watermark: avg: 601K, p25: 2K, p50: 2K, p75: 2048K, p90: 2048K, p95: 2048K)  
``` 

(This is from one of the benchmarks that purposefully creates very large goroutines mixed with small goroutines.)

The CL commit message has more detail. The code itself could use a bit more cleanup. The logic is basically the same as ~April when I tested it a decent amount, but I did just tweak things slightly as part of a clean up pass, so I would want to stress test it again a bit more myself before Uber tries it out.

One other quick comment is my "more aggressive" CL is also has a histogram to support percentiles (re-using what I did in one my earlier CLs), which can help for example for a bimodal distribution, but that is also an example of something that might be able to be simplified or dropped if the data hints it is not needed.

// eh, it turns out I typed this in, but I didn't send. So chronologically this comment is 48h old.

Hey @randall77 @mknyszek  - would you be able to give a yay/nay on the patch above? We're about to start a fleet-wide rollout, we'd rather roll out something "closer to the future reality" as opposed to "this will never land" :) 

We've:
- rolled this out to 30+ services - including some "risky/high-rps/high-goroutines" ones 
- stack copy cost virtually disappears (~0.2% now, from ~4%)
- no noticeable RSS impact, stack size grew in some services by the expected ~8mb/process.

We do like the minimal complication, the fact that we're reusing existing machinery, that we're addressing the root of the problem (let similar goroutines reuse the stack as it becomes available), and that it works for shorter-than-gc-lived goroutines. We fear that the 128kb/P might be a bit much for the runtime, but also we're only "growing" memory if the application needed it earlier (i.e., shallow goroutines do not suffer).

@thepudds thanks! This looks ... slightly intimidating, though. Will need to parse carefully :)

I am sympathetic to the problem that we're measuring stack sizes only at GC. If one has a large pile of small, ~always blocked goroutines, that brings down the average, even though they don't contribute to the cost of creating+growing stacks at all. So something that considers dynamic creation/destruction more directly, rather than a snapshot of existing goroutine sizes, would be good.

That said, I'm not a big fan of just putting free goroutines with >min stacks in the cache. That could cause problems with other goroutine population patterns. For instance, if we have short-lived goroutines that are mostly small, but rarely need to call some subroutine that uses lots of stack, then eventually the rare thing happens on all the stacks in the cache, and then everything is running with a large stack, mostly unnecessarily. And stack shrinking wouldn't ameliorate that problem much.

If we kept some sort of statistics at goroutine exit, maybe we could approximate how much growth is actually happening. At exit we can't get exact stack usage (like we can at GC time), but the allocated size is within a factor of 2 of the high water mark usage at least (when born+died in the same GC cycle).

Thanks for your response @randall77!

@thepudds  - I ran the watermarking patch on 2 of our services, the logs can be found in [here](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1tUtHJoG6hZSDapa-DgL5SruNWiYTO_YM?usp=sharing). 

Here's the results & observations I made: 

Service | runtime.copystack share (stackcache) | runtime.copystack share (watermarking, without the printString)
-- | -- | --
Service-1 | 0.11% | 5.2-7.4%
Service-2 | 3.1% | 3.2-3.4%

Most traced goroutines die within one GC generation. The `gdestroy` instrumentation successfully captures their peak watermark, so short-lived goroutine data is not lost.

In Service-1, however, the goroutine population is bursty. Some GC intervals contain mostly growers, while others contain a very large population of small-stack goroutines. During the latter intervals, growers can fall below 10% of the histogram, causing the global p90 watermark to become small.

The resulting feedback is one GC cycle behind: a grower-heavy interval raises startingStackSize for the following cohort, but that cohort may be mostly small goroutines. Their samples then lower it before the next grower-heavy burst.
Concretely, Service-1’s averaging calculation remained around 4 KiB, while watermarking selected 32 KiB, then 16 KiB, and finally 4 KiB as the watermark p90 dropped to 2 KiB.

As a first experiment, I plan to rate-limit downward adjustments: increases will still take effect at the next GC, but decreases will be limited to one size class per GC. For example, 32→16 KiB rather than 32→4 KiB. I’ll measure both copystack CPU and the additional stack-memory cost.
